courseName: OCR Level 3 Cambridge Advanced National (AAQ) in Human Biology · Unit F172: Genetics (Topic Area 3 / NEA Task 2)
ocrSpec: Topic Area 3.3.1 (Privacy & ethical issues in genetic testing) + 3.3.2 (Concerns about storage of DNA on a DNA database)
focus: Addressing Clinical Confidentiality, Genetic Information Sharing, DNA Database Storage Risks, Insurance/Employment Discrimination, Result Accuracy, and Bioethical Dilemmas for Ben (P10)
deliverable: 75-minute classroom deck grounded in RCPath/RCP/BSGM guidance, UK GDPR, Equality Act 2010, and the ABI Insurance Code, equipping learners to thoroughly address at least two privacy issues and at least two ethical issues for Ben (P10) — plus DNA database governance (3.3.2).

objectives.knowledge: Explain how privacy and ethical issues arise in genetic testing (confidentiality, sharing, DNA storage, consequences of positive results, false/uncertain results) and why each matters (3.3.1).
objectives.application: Explain the specific concerns surrounding storage of DNA on national or commercial DNA databases (surveillance, genetic discrimination, and non-100% accuracy of DNA evidence) and how safeguards minimise them (3.3.2).
objectives.evaluation: Explain clearly how at least two privacy issues and at least two ethical issues can be practically addressed for Ben as the patient under UK clinical and legal frameworks (P10).

terminology.def: RCPath/RCP/BSGM principle recognising that while medical records are confidential to the individual, genetic data is inherently familial and may carry life-altering relevance for biological relatives.

UK clinical pathway when a patient refuses to warn at-risk relatives: (1) encourage voluntary sharing, (2) offer anonymised sharing, (3) MDT ethics review & minimum necessary disclosure only if serious preventable harm outweighs confidentiality.

terminology.term: ABI Code on Genetic Testing & Insurance
terminology.def: UK voluntary moratorium protecting patients from disclosing predictive genetic test results to insurers — with one notable exception for Huntington's disease on life insurance policies exceeding £500,000.
Core bioethical principle of patient autonomy protecting asymptomatic individuals (including Ben's children until age 18) from being forced to learn unrequested predictive genetic risk.

Unfair treatment by employers, insurers, or state agencies using stored genomic data, mitigated via UK GDPR/Data Protection Act 2018, Equality Act 2010, strict access controls, and data destruction rights.

theoryPoints: OCR P10 Mandatory Minimum (Patient Focus — Ben): Must explain how AT LEAST TWO privacy issues AND AT LEAST TWO ethical issues can be addressed for Ben — and provide an explicit rationale if any spec issue is deemed non-relevant to Ben's scenario.

Privacy Issues & UK Solutions (Spec 3.3.1): (1) Confidentiality of medical/genetic records → NHS Caldicott Principles, encrypted EHRs, UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018 restricted access; (2) Sharing of familial genetic data → explicit informed consent, anonymised family letter options; (3) Storage of DNA samples & genomic records → Human Tissue Act 2004 consent, pseudonymised NHS biobank governance, right to request sample destruction; (4) Employment & Insurance consequences → Equality Act 2010 (reasonable workplace adjustments for Ben's teaching role, protection from unfair dismissal) & UK ABI Code on Genetic Testing & Insurance (note HD £500k life insurance rule!).

Ethical Issues & Clinical Resolution (Spec 3.3.1 & RCPath): (1) Autonomy vs Duty to Warn relatives → RCPath stepped protocol (persuasion → anonymised disclosure → MDT review); note Ben's adoption adds nuance regarding unknown biological relatives; (2) Consequences of positive test & psychological harm → mandatory pre-/post-test counselling & mental health safety planning; (3) Testing of minors & 'Right Not to Know' → defer predictive testing of Ben's 6yo & 3yo until legal capacity (age 18); (4) Accuracy, false results & intermediate CAG grey zones (27–35 / 36–39 repeats) → UKAS-accredited NHS labs, duplicate sample confirmation, repeat-sizing QA, clear counselling on reduced penetrance.

DNA Database Storage Concerns & Safeguards (Spec 3.3.2): (1) Surveillance (familial searching, police/state/commercial tracking via DTC sites like GEDmatch) → statutory oversight, strict opt-in consent, deletion of innocent profiles under Protection of Freedoms Act 2012; (2) Genetic discrimination (third-party data leaks/commercial resale) → zero commercial sharing in NHS Genomic Medicine Service, encryption, legal bans; (3) DNA evidence is NOT 100% accurate (sample contamination, lab swap, partial/degraded profiles, mosaicism/chimerism, match probability misinterpretation) → chain-of-custody protocols, independent confirmatory testing, corroborating clinical/non-DNA evidence.

workedExample.title: Structuring a Watertight P10 Response for Ben (≥2 Privacy + ≥2 Ethical Issues)
workedExample.subtitle: Issue → Why It Arises for Ben → Concrete UK Clinical / Legal Solution

steps.label: Privacy Issue 1 — NHS Confidentiality & Workplace Protection
steps.detail: Arises because Ben is a teacher fearing stigma or dismissal if his school learns of his HD diagnosis. Addressed via NHS confidentiality/UK GDPR (no disclosure to employer without Ben's written consent) and the Equality Act 2010 (legal protection from discrimination + right to reasonable adjustments when he chooses to disclose).

steps.label: Privacy Issue 2 — DNA Storage & Insurance Safeguards
steps.detail: Arises because Ben's extracted DNA and genomic data are stored in NHS labs and he has a young family needing financial security. Addressed via Human Tissue Act 2004 explicit storage consent, pseudonymised secure NHS databases (never sold commercially), and guidance on the UK ABI Insurance Code (including the £500,000 HD predictive threshold vs diagnostic disclosure rules).

steps.label: Ethical Issues 1 & 2 — Autonomy/Duty to Warn & Result Accuracy/Psychological Harm
steps.detail: Issue A (Confidentiality vs Duty to Warn): Under RCPath guidance, Ben's genetic counsellor encourages voluntary open dialogue with his wife while strictly deferring predictive testing of his 6yo & 3yo children until age 18 to protect their 'right not to know'. Issue B (Accuracy & Psychological Impact): Addressed via UKAS-accredited NHS duplicate confirmatory PCR testing (eliminating sample-swap false positives) paired with structured pre-/post-test psychological counselling.

hingeQuestions.question: Under RCPath / RCP / BSGM clinical genetics guidance, what is the FIRST step a genetic counsellor should take if a patient initially refuses to share a serious heritable diagnosis with at-risk relatives?
options: Immediately telephone the patient's employer and wider family without telling the patient

Actively explore the patient's fears, encourage voluntary communication ('genetic solidarity'), and discuss anonymised information-sharing options before ever considering an MDT breach of confidentiality
Delete the patient's genetic test results from the NHS record
Publish the patient's pedigree in a public research database
hingeQuestions.explanation: Confidentiality is a primary duty but not absolute. RCPath mandates a stepped approach: encourage voluntary disclosure first, consider anonymised sharing second, and only breach confidentiality after MDT consultation to prevent serious avoidable harm, informing the patient beforehand.

hingeQuestions.question: Which of the following accurately explains why DNA database evidence is NOT 100% accurate (Topic Area 3.3.2)?
options: Humans have completely identical DNA across every chromosome

Sample contamination, laboratory mislabelling, partial/degraded profiles, somatic mosaicism, and prosecutor's fallacy misinterpretation of random match probabilities can all cause false inclusions or exclusions
DNA completely degrades inside living human blood cells within 24 hours
PCR amplifies proteins instead of nucleic acids
hingeQuestions.explanation: Technical errors (contamination, sample mix-up, partial degraded samples) and biological/statistical realities (identical twins, chimerism, coincidental partial matches) mean DNA database records require chain-of-custody verification and corroborating evidence.

plenary: P10 focuses strictly on the patient (Ben) and requires clear solutions for ≥2 privacy issues and ≥2 ethical issues — plus explicit justification for any excluded issue.
UK safeguards work together: NHS Caldicott/UK GDPR confidentiality, Equality Act 2010, Human Tissue Act 2004, ABI Insurance Code, and RCPath's stepped disclosure protocol.

Topic Area 3.3.2 DNA database concerns (surveillance, discrimination, non-100% accuracy) are minimised through strict informed consent, statutory deletion rules, pseudonymisation, and confirmatory lab QA.
